33.t: First trumpet, hearing Brunies in Biloxi, and the Alamo theater pit under Tasso
33.s: His father gave him a trumpet at ten; he recalls hearing Abbie and Merritt Brunies, playing the symphony, and his muted trumpet feature in the Alamo pit, praised in the press.
33.ch: Early career, theaters and Cobb's Tea Room
33.q: Never forget music. I love music. My father gave me a trumpet when I was 10 years of age. He went off and came back that afternoon and I played America for him. On the trumpet. I don't know, I must have had a natural ambiture. Because right now I can just get about eight notes out of my horn and I…

33.t: Violin, piano and trumpet lessons with Paulin Fabian
33.s: He played violin well enough to double, studied trumpet with a former Republican Guard Band musician, and earned $8 at his first engagement at 12.
33.q: I never heard of him. My brother was a trombonist. I played the violin fairly well, enough to double. And I attempted piano, just for the harmony, you know. But I had the finest trumpet teacher in the world. He was a member of the Republican Guard Band of France. He came here with the French Opera…

33.t: School years and playing fiddle and trumpet at the tin roof dance job
33.s: DeDroit graduated high school in 1910 and tells of his father's dance band and how he switched from fiddle to trumpet at a dance hall called the tin roof.
33.ch: Strings, arrangements and the Shrine band
33.q: a case in point, I played it. Now, as I explained to you before, when I was going to school I wasn't waiting to study. You know what I'm saying? Mm-hmm. We had a dance job. My father had a dance job. My father was a band leader and a contract. And it was out of what we called a tin roof. There's a…

101.t: The garden-hose trumpet and the neighbours' pawnshop horn
101.s: Terry builds a pretend trumpet from garden hose and the neighbours buy him a $12.50 pawnshop horn.
101.q: I sure did. I was so carried away with the trumpet, and of course in a big family, we’re – it’s a problem to feed and clothe kids. I wanted a horn, so I couldn’t buy a horn. My dad wouldn’t think of buying – couldn’t think of buying me a horn, so I went to the dump – city dump – and found me an old…

101.t: First instruction: Sy's tuba fingering and valve trombone at Vashon
101.s: Terry learns fingering from Sy and gets a valve trombone from the teacher at Vashon High before a trumpet is free.
101.q: Not until I went to high school, because I didn’t know anything about music, except what I would listen to and what my brother-in-law Sy occasionally, when he had

101.t: Waiting for a trumpet at Vashon High
101.s: Playing marches on valve trombone, mastering scales, and getting the trumpet next semester.
101.q: At this particular time, it was only marches, because I didn’t want to get into anything too heavy with the valve trombone. I’m waiting on this trumpet, so I’m just biding the time, just mastering the scales [Terry sings three ascending major scales]. That’s all I wanted to do, is get them scales…

87.s: He tried trumpet and drums before the trombone, which he first played seriously at school in 1926 and took lessons on later.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: I fooled around with trumpet a while. It just got a little too rough for me. And I fooled around with drums a little while but --

87.t: Hearing Pryor in concert; buying his first trombone
87.s: He heard Pryor at band concerts in Richmond and Washington and bought his first trombone in a Washington pawn shop.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: I heard him in the band concert in Washington, D. C. Yeah, that's where I heard him. And I heard him at a band concert before that in Richmond, Virginia, in the '20's, about '28. And he didn't play -- he couldn't play any jazz. And he couldn't do a lot of little tricks that I had learned to do --…

87.t: Fooling around with instruments in Savannah
87.s: He hung around local musicians, played with Georgia Red's trombone, and thought the old blues players were the best.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: Yeah, well, I knew -- I knew a few musicians around Savannah and they played instruments. And they didn't play them very well but they played them, you know. And I used to hang around some of these musicians. I was just a kid.

677.t: Finding the trombone and the idea of playing melody
677.s: He tried the church choir leader's trombone, got lessons from his school orchestra leader, and decided the trombone should play melodies like a cello rather than tailgate style.
677.q: Now, as I said before, my father being a minister, we were continually shifting around and different things, and the choir leader of our church was a trombone player, and he used to use his trombone only on Sunday, and so it stayed up in the vestibule of the church. And I keep -- kept noticing this…

677.t: High school bands and intensive practice in San Francisco
677.s: In school orchestras and a noon-hour dance band, with a strict father who allowed only church music, he practised melodic playing for hours; he recalls bandmate Phil Lambert.
677.q: much music, I couldn't -- I didn't keep track of dates too well. I just knew that I wasn't -- I was in grammar school into high school, and by this time I had gotten so I could play in the grammar school orchestra on trombone and the high school orches- tras on trombone, and of course my father was…

677.t: Tuba, solos at church, then violin
677.s: In Oakland he borrowed a tuba through the school system, played "Silent Night" at nine or ten, then took up violin from a church lady's gift.
677.q: I really started on tuba. Possibly an explanation of why I started on the various instruments is because in Oakland, California, they had a very good school system, and if your parent would sign a bond, you could take out any instrument that you wanted to learn. And so I took out tuba, and I stayed…

69.t: First lessons, school trombone and the Municipal Band
69.s: Taught solfege by his uncle, Juan was given a trombone at school and then joined the Municipal Band on euphonium, occasionally playing third trombone.
69.q: Oh, I guess I was about 18 years old. He taught me how to do solfege (unintelligible), you know? And then I learned my instrument in school. They gave me a trombone, and I knew, by being around my uncle with the Municipal Band, I

69.t: Playing for visiting opera and Pavlova's ballet
69.s: The New York opera company and Pavlova's ballet visited San Juan, and his uncle slipped him into the trombone section even though he was still learning.
69.q: No, from New York. The regular opera company, like with Anna Pavlova and things like that -- oh, they came from New York. The best, and the best directors, and so forth.

69.t: Trombone instead of violin; Rose adds that his uncle taught him everything
69.s: He was handed a trombone at school, dropped violin because trombone paid in dance orchestras, and Rose reminds him of his uncle's teaching.
69.q: Well, that I cannot say. Also, I played violin in the orchestra in school. Yeah, I was learning violin, but it was a little too hard, and I dropped it, you know? Because with the trombone, then I started playing in the orchestra for the dancers and so forth, and I was making a little bit of money,…

94.t: First trumpet at Phoenix Indian School and his side-of-the-mouth embouchure
94.s: He first took up the trumpet in 1923; it slipped to one side of his mouth, and teachers later told him to leave it that way.
94.q: Yes, when I went to the Phoenix Indian School in 1923. That's where I first picked up the trumpet. And, incidentally, when I picked up the trumpet, it always slipped to one side of my embouchure. And that's how I happen to this day play on the side of my mouth.

94.t: Starting trombone in the Tucson High School orchestra
94.s: With the concert band full, he took a $12 trombone for the high school orchestra and has played it ever since.
94.q: Yes. I tell ya how I got to the trombone. I, I went to the band master in Tucson High School, and they were all filled up, every instrument, and I couldn't, I couldn't join the concert band. So they said, "However, we have an opening for a trombonist if you play trombone, we have a opening for a --…

94.t: Sherman Institute at Riverside, where he started jazz trombone
94.s: He applied to Sherman Institute in California after his stepfather died, played jazz in the dormitory, and had no particular trombone models.
94.q: Well, I didn't, perform any, any -- I wasn't good enough. I was good enough to be in the orchestra in the high school, but I didn't get to playing jazz until I -- that year, 1930. it was the year 1930 when my step-father died, and I said I might as well go to the Indian school. And that'd be one,…

473.t: Hence Grundy's advice and being given an alto horn
473.s: Trombonist Hence Grundy told his mother the band would give a trombone and free lessons; at the band Jones's arms proved too short for seventh position, so Mrs. Allen gave him an alto horn.
473.ch: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
473.q: He played with a band called the Noble Blue Guitar Stompers, and he played with a jug band. We used to have a jug band. You know, how you blow on the jug? (Singing).

473.t: The mellophone year and quick rise to first trumpet
473.s: Mrs. Allen bought four mellophones; he played one for a year using his alto mouthpiece, then went to trumpet and in about two years was first trumpet.
473.ch: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
473.q: See, what we did was two years on the alto horn, but one year -- just about, not exactly, but one year I played the alto horn, and we were breaking them up so fast, and then we come in one day after about a year and she had four mellophones. See, there was four of us playing alto horn, and she had…

473.t: Moving up to trumpet as older players leave
473.s: After about two years on alto horn, first-chair Matthew Holland left to play with adult bands; chairs shifted up and Jones was given fourth trumpet and quickly rose to first chair.
473.ch: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
473.q: Yeah, about two years on the alto, and some the guys left. There was a guy named Matthew Holland, he was the first chair man, and he studied very hard at home on his horn, and finally he went out and started playing with the adults around town, you know.

173.t: Joining a boys' brass band under Professor Telesco
173.s: A group of boys starts a brass band; Joe Telesco teaches them eight bars at a time on clarinet. Stecklet starts on cornet around age 19 with no prior lessons.
173.q: Well, I was born in 1877, and about 21 years, 19 years, to be exact, when I started fooling around music. But I was quick, I was learning very, very fast.

173.s: He bought a Conn cornet, probably on Canal Street.
173.q: Well, I got a, a Korn instrument. A Korn. G.W. Korn, I think, was the proper initial. I think it's G.W. Korn. And where'd you buy it? I may be mistaken, but it was a Korn instrument. C-O-N-N. Yeah, C.G. Korn. C.G. Well, let's not see. Where'd you get, where'd you buy it? I got that from, well, I…

241.t: Valve trombone, slide trombone and brass band playing
241.s: He played valve trombone when learning in Reserve but never in a band, played some slide trombone at home, and played trumpet in brass bands.
241.q: Yeah, I played it. When I first, when I first, when I first started playing, learning that play, I was learning that play. It was reserve. Yeah, reserve.

241.t: Teaching himself trumpet and the first three-number band
241.s: He had no method; he started on valve trombone, settled on trumpet and learned one number at a time until a small club band could play three numbers all night.
241.q: I didn't have no method when I first started. Mm-hmm. No, you see I started, I started my, just myself, you know, just, you know, pick up the horn and play, you know. Well, first I started playing on, on trombone. Mm-hmm. First, I was on the key trombone, the valve. Mm-hmm. Then after that, I took…

182.t: Buying his first cornet from a music store
182.s: He recalls buying his first cornet and method book from an old man's music store on Chartres Street, before World War I.
182.q: Yeah, one of these. Yeah, yeah. A little sharp carnet. Yeah, the first carnet I bought, over here on, uh, right from here, uh, let me see, you don't know, uh, what street that, uh, what that furniture place right in front of you? Oh, yeah, I know. It, it, it had a ice house. Yeah, where that ice…

182.t: Fess's uncle on slide trombone; taking Fess and Peter on jobs
182.s: Tom names the first slide trombone he saw and recalls taking the young Fess, Peter and Manuel to jobs in the cane cart, with violin relieving his swollen lips.
182.ch: Early bands and the city, c. 1898-1900s
182.q: Yeah, playing violin. Yeah. He didn't even tie it, but I never did. He used to come over there and play it when I was young, you understand? Mm-hm. Used to be around first. Well I was the first one taking him and Peeta on the job. He used to come over there and play when I was young, you…

48.t: Why he chose trombone: the circus trombonists
48.s: He decided to imitate a trombonist in a circus side show, met George Williams, and discusses lower-position playing.
48.q: I don't know, I take my liking to trombone. There was a show that came into New Orleans, and they had two trombones. And I noticed a fellow that was playing trombone. He was quick and fast, and he could handle that trombone faster. Well, when I first started, I told fellows I was going to imitate…

48.t: Age to start trombone; slide trumpet
48.s: Starting at eight, positions, and sliding trumpets tried by Oliver and others.
48.q: A real little kid can teach it, could he? Yeah, you can start a little kid. You can start, well, about, say about eight years old. You can start a kid eight years old. And he'll make it. Like the violin.

5.t: The first cornet, bought for a dollar and a half
5.s: He recalls buying a short second-hand cornet for $1.50 in a junk store and keeping it a good while.
5.q: No, I don't remember the make of that one, but I do remember where the place I bought it was an old store that sold everything. Just sort of like a junk second hand store.

5.t: Getting a cornet from a neighbor boy at ten or eleven
5.s: A neighbor boy let him blow his trumpet, the boy's father taught him the scale, and he got a cornet at about ten or eleven.
5.q: Well, I was a boy of just about my age, lived next door to me, had a trumpet, and we used to play together, you know, kids together. Yeah. And he used to let me blow on the horn. So that's how I got started on the... Blowing on his horn.

881.t: Coming to Chicago at 15 and starting the trombone at 18
881.s: He arrived at about 15, started to play at about 18 with good teachers, and joined the union in 1921.
881.ch: Becoming a player; Rene, Bunk and Armstrong
881.q: No, no I wasn't thinking about playing. And what gave you the idea of playing? My mother wanted me to play. Well she wanted you to play. Yeah, yeah.

881.t: How he came to the trombone and the first Chicago band with Bernie Young
881.s: Joe Oliver suggested clarinet but his mother bought a trombone; he studied with William Robinson, formed a band with Bernie Young and the Simeons, joined the union, and learned from Dutrey around Oliver's circle.
881.q: Well, my first instrument was trombone, but it wasn't my favorite instrument. I'd like to tell you, Bill, about how I come to study the trombone. While talking with Joe Oliver, it must have been somewhere around 1920, 1921, somewhere along there. He, I told Joe Oliver that I was going to take…

644.t: Playing the district as a boy in short pants, starting on trumpet
644.s: He went into the district at 14 or 15, wearing long pants over his short ones, and says he started on trumpet.
644.ch: Early life and the New Orleans band scene
644.q: In the district, I was in short pants. To go to work at night time, I'd have to put long pants on top of my short pants. Because you wasn't allowed. Nobody, no. Yep. Well, this wasn't allowed in the district with short pants. I'd wear them, you remember the old days? We'd wear stockings. I'd put a…

644.t: Old trumpet and trombone players, Tony Parenti and Santo
644.s: Lala recalls playing around 1905-1910 and the trombonists and clarinettists he started, including Tony Parenti and the story of a boy's first trombone.
644.q: We used to play trumpet. We used to play trumpet. Yeah, that's right. And me and I played in 1905, 1910. 1910. Perfect. And I had more trumpet players, man. I joined out, man. I'm getting wet out.

56.t: First meeting Bolden at the New Orleans music store
56.s: While trying his new trombone, Ory was heard by Bolden, who invited him to join, but his sister refused.
56.ch: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
56.q: How old were you? Do you remember? Fourteen. Well, uh... You said. I was, uh... You see, I was ten, played a job at the old horn. I guess it picked me. I was about eleven years old. It was a year later, I bought the horn, you know? Where, where did you meet Bolden? I was, uh... I just bought my…

56.t: First job at ten and the cheap first valve trombone
56.s: Ory played up and down the road to Baton Rouge from age ten; his first horn cost $4 and had holes plastered with soap.
56.q: Well, I was on the stand playing when I was 10 years old. I played my first job when I was 10 years old. Ten. Played for a big... Playing regular Val trombone. Val trombone. All the real instruments. Mm-hmm.

909.t: Eddie Atkins and Ernest Kelly as models
909.s: Morris came up under Eddie Atkins and Ernest Kelly; Kelly's trombone made him want to learn it, and he first played a little cornet.
909.ch: Childhood and early music in Algiers
909.q: Yeah And Ernest Kelly I was under him That's why I wanted to learn Trambone Because Ernest Kelly was playing trambone And I loved the trambone Yeah, so That's why I used to try to play cornette I was a good little cornette player, you know But not for out Just for myself And now and then I would…

909.t: Taking up trombone with Brady's instruments
909.s: He started on cornet but preferred trombone, taking it up at eighteen to twenty on a cheap slide instrument Brady bought for the band.
909.q: Well, I'll tell you the truth I got a piece of that trombone now Got it right there in that drawer Piece of it here That show you how long I mean there

28.t: Switching from clarinet to trumpet at Manual School
28.s: Because the clarinet lacked the melody he moved to trumpet as his second instrument, played in the Manual School orchestra and won valedictorian honours playing Ave Maria.
28.q: All right. We did this say about six months, then I'm feeling good now, so I was going to school and then I was -- there was a boy named Arthur Lanier on the clarinet. I liked the clarinet and I was still studying the clarinet but I was playing the second part on the trumpet, so then I found that…

28.t: Ukulele, Emmy Lucas and working toward a clarinet
28.s: At about thirteen he played ukulele and was told by the strict pianist Emmy Lucas to study; he was saving for a clarinet when he was sent to Louisiana on vacation.
28.q: So it seems like, I was going to school and everything and then I think I was about 13 -- I had a little ukele and was playing it (unintelligible) and there was a man named Emmy Lucas, he worked down through Harditch's Brewery and they sent him to school and he was a genius. He knew all the music,…

232.t: Buying a three-dollar trombone and joining the Tuskegee second band
232.s: Hearing the Tuskegee band makes him want a horn; Owens finds him a trombone and Captain Frank Dryer has it repaired and puts him in the second band.
232.q: The thing was these were what we called natives. They had money and got into something and were very careless around. Anyway, I entered school and went onto school and everything was going on there and then nicely and then when I'd get to hear the orchestra, to go into the dining room, and that…

232.t: Learning trombone with William Moore at the power plant
232.s: Studying applied electricity, he works summer shifts at the power plant with clarinetist William Moore, who drills him on music, and Captain Dryer rewards him with a new Conn trombone.
232.q: a clarinet player, a very fine musician and by me working up my way and everything, I was staying--I wasn't coming home then, so I was going to work all that summer

91.t: Buying a trumpet on layaway, Cuban Bennett and Bubber Miley
91.s: He wanted to play trumpet, inspired by his cousin Cuban Bennett and neighbor Bubber Miley, and paid $33 off at a dollar a week.
91.q: Well, the instrument that I had at that particular time was a saxophone, although I had started with a trumpet -- because I had given up on the piano. I sort of felt that I wanted to play a wind instrument, and the instrument I wanted to play was really the trumpet. I had a cousin whose name was…

91.t: Eugene Mikell, Harold Proctor and the layaway trumpet retold
91.s: Carter retells how Harold Proctor and Cuban Bennett and Miley led him to a layaway trumpet bought for $33.
91.q: But I don't know if I ever mentioned that to you before, Jim. Well, Hal Proctor was the fellow that lived up the street from me. Oh, he was probably 15 or 20 years older than I me, and he played saxophone. Now after my trying to play I had... now, I had had some piano lessons from my mother and…

79.t: Starting on cornet instead of trumpet
79.s: Thomas explains why a cornet is easier for a child to balance than a trumpet.
79.ch: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work
79.q: Well, he started us off and the difference from a kid learning an instrument like a cornet or trumpet, I found it is the balance. It's hard for a kid with small hands to balance the trumpet where a cornet is easier to balance and it makes him feel closer to the instrument.

79.t: How the kids were assigned instruments
79.s: Langford came out weekly. At the first meeting at Mr. Sims' home, the boys chose instruments, and Thomas, looking husky, was told he was the cornet player. They still scheduled swimming around rehearsals.
79.ch: Boyhood in Webster Groves and early roadhouse work
79.q: Each week. We lived across from the school. That's where our home is now, my brother's home and each week he'd come out to Webster Groves and give us our instruction. Now we first went to Mr. Sims' home where we first got together and the selection of this thing was a gasser. He said, 'Well, what…

172.t: Switching to trombone, Lambert, Welch and joining the Silver Leaf Band
172.s: Umphrey advises a trombone; the band breaks up and reforms under Henry Lambert and Frank Welch, who brings them to Albert Batiste's Silver Leaf Band.
172.q: About one mile and a quarter out of the city limit. And we used to have to meet Professor Umphrey every Sunday morning about 9 o'clock. We had a little road cart. We'd carry him, flurry and two. And so the people that I wait for, they give us a place that we could have our practice, take our…

854.t: Buying the horn at twenty dollars and Jack Lane's band
854.s: Where and for how much he bought the horn at about age 18, and that Jack Lane was already going strong.
854.q: Yeah, I bought my, my horn at a place they called Uncle Joe, down on Ramport Street. Okay, $12 for it. And I started out then, it was about, I was about 20. I was about, well, I actually was, no, I was about 18 years old when I started.

868.t: Starting on trumpet: cousin Ran Briscoe's horn and early lessons
868.s: De De got his first trumpet at about fifteen from a cousin on the road via her sister, then took lessons; the sister later played in Sweetheart's Rhythm girl band.
868.q: No, no, no, no, no. It started, I had a niece, cousin rather, on the road years ago. I was around about fifteen. With a regular, a minister or a troop, whatever they call it, traveling around, you know. And she played trumpet. In other words, taking sick or what, she sent the trumpet to her sister,…

20.t: The Entertainers' owners and the birthday trumpet
20.s: The club is run by two Sicilians; the band buys Lee his first trumpet for his birthday.
20.q: So, this entertainer was run by two Sicilians, Johnny Latters and Joe Latters. Used to be named Old Hunt and One Ranch where Joe Oliver used to play. Yeah. And all the good boys in the good old days. Packed every night, packed every night. We'd close everything down in that part. So, I got tangled…

687.s: He started in carnival bands, brass bands and medicine shows, on alto horn, bass horn and baritone, then trombone and a little saxophone in New Orleans.
687.q: well my experiences came early they came in carnival bands brass bands medicine shows and high school you know school bands high school bands and orchestras were secondary

244.t: From bugle corps to a pawn-shop trumpet
244.s: The band was dissolved; around 1930 he bought a beat-up trumpet for about $15.
244.q: Yes. Why did you do that? after the band, they broke up the band from the Item Tribune, well, they had two bands, the white band was big, was a huge band and they had trumpets and everything in that, they had a real big band

709.t: Parents, learning trombone from Professor Humphrey, the Elks band
709.s: His parents were Baptist churchgoers and played no music. Kelly took up valve trombone at 21 to 23 in the brass band, taught by Professor Humphrey, in the band called the Elks.
709.ch: Early life and the plantation brass band
709.q: Valorant of Liberty. That's why he was. That was my professor. He teached me eyes and bones, pure ants and all of us.

860.t: Forming the Crane River Jazz Band; New York jazz heard at sea
860.s: Colyer learned trumpet in the merchant navy and formed the Crane River band c. 1948-49; he recalls hearing the Condon band in New York and first playing at Cranford.
860.ch: British revival and the Crane River band
860.q: of all that you formed well that was a crane river jazz band I came out of the merchant Navy I learned to play trumpet at sea when I was in the merchant Navy then when I came out I formed the crane river jazz band yes what year was that I think that was uh I'm many 48 49 yes um when you learned…

816.t: Birth and first lessons on a borrowed brass horn
816.s: Warner gives his birth date and tells how his half-brother, a Dutrey pupil, put a small brass horn in his hands and taught him three positions at about 22.
816.q: New Orleans, Louisiana. December 31st, 1890. I first started learning music with a half-brother mine. He learned from Honoré Dutré. Well, when he left, before he left, he bought him a new trombone. And a boy wanted to buy his old trombone from him. And he refused to sell it to him. He paid one…

568.t: Roy Palmer brings him a brass horn
568.s: After two summers Roy Palmer brought him a horn, which he polished with brass polish and started fooling with.
568.q: No, I don't know this guitar player either because he was a very sensible fellow. He didn't drink and he didn't smoke, you see. And he tried to carry the band on straight. Well, I kept that place going for two summers. And after then I started playing music. Roy Palmer brought me a horn. And the…

864.t: The tin flute and the cornet from Prechter
864.s: He first played a six-hole tin flute; a white man named Prechter gave him an old cornet, which he never mastered.
864.q: Well, I'll tell you. Helped you? When I first started to try to play, I used to play a flute. You know those ten flutes? Oh, yeah. When I was so good on them, everybody tried to encourage me to play music. At that time things were so hard, I mean I never could buy an instrument, you see? But I…

873.t: Getting started: lessons and playing with Alexander's band at 14
873.s: No family musicians; boys bought instruments, took lessons from Robichaud and Cleven Williams, then played with Dejean Alexander's seven-piece band, moving from piano scores to orchestrations.
873.q: Well, back to the music business. How did you get started? Were any of your family musicals that helped you out? No, no one. I started, like I said, the other night, a bunch of boys got together and... started a little band, organized a little band. I don't work in a few months at all. Somebody…

42.t: Learning trombone and buying a cornet at school
42.s: He played trombone and cornet in the school band at Campbell College and bought a secondhand cornet at 16.
42.ch: Growing up with jazz in Belfast
42.q: no I didn't I'm trying to I was about 16 15 or 16 when I took up the trombone to play with uh this little band we had in uh high school at Campbell College and we played around I played the corny at the same time I didn't I didn't own an instrument these were all you know instruments owned by the…

187.t: First altos, then trombone lessons with Claiborne Williams
187.s: He started on alto horn around 16, admired his cousin's trombone playing, and learned breathing from Professor Williams; joined George Nelson's six-piece band.
187.q: No, I started playing on altos. One of those straight altos, you know? Altos. I started poop, poop, peck, peck on, as they called it. You understand? And from then, then I took up—

46.t: Moving to Chicago and choosing the trombone
46.s: The family moved to Chicago about 1920; he wanted trumpet, but his cousin took it, so he got a mail-order trombone and rode the L to lessons.
46.q: I taken up music after I moved to Chicago. Yeah, that, we moved to Chicago possibly, it was in 19 or 20. I'm not, I'm not sure. It's very vague because I was still very young at that time.

828.s: He took up music at about 17; a cousin gave him a violin but Humphrey steered him to trombone.
828.q: I have brothers, but none of them didn't take up no music. And I didn't take up music until around 1919. At that time I was around 17, 17 years old. And I started on the trombone. The trombone. And I was taking lessons from Professor J.B. Humphrey. Oh yes. Jim Humphrey. Jim Humphrey.

875.t: Buying his first cornet for five dollars
875.s: He buys a cornet from a neighbour of the curio shop and Chris Kelly shows him his first scale.
875.q: Well I got the first instrument when I was working at the carolero store on Canelo Street. They had the King Dentist next door and there was a fellow, he was trying to learn the cornet. It was the cornet when I first played. And so he asked me if I wanted to buy it. So I told him no, I was playing…

675.t: First instruments and trombone in a medicine show
675.s: Braud began on violin and mandolin, played trombone in a Chicago medicine show in 1918, and was too young for the district.
675.q: Violin and mandolin. Oh, man. And I played a little guitar. And in 1918, I played on a medicine show, Trombone, in Chicago. That's when I started my first

570.t: Trombone lessons and uncle Chester Morrison's drum set
570.s: He briefly took trombone on a neighbour's instrument, but stayed with drums; an uncle bought his first real set.
570.q: Well, Mr. Bill, I did take lessons to play tramo on. But I got back on my drums. I liked it in my drums. This is in Morgan City? Yeah, in Morgan City. But I liked it in my drums and I just went on back and it's on my drums. I didn't stay off them that long. And I had an uncle in the country by the…

283.t: St. Mary's Italian band and buying his first trombone
283.s: He and Tony Parenti played in an Italian band; he started on another horn, was steered to trombone, got lessons and a nine-dollar horn, and a neighbour heard him practicing.
283.q: Oh sure, we went to school together and we started together. We played an Italian band at St. Mary's Church, you know? Oh yeah. They had an Italian band that used to rehearse in the backyard, had a big room there. In fact, when I first started there I played peclone I see, instead of trombone. I…

285.t: Starting age, father's cornet and the Tosseau nickname
285.s: He started around 16, had borrowed his father's cornet earlier, was nicknamed after bandleader Emile Tosseau, and taught himself by ear.
285.q: Armand Vesey, Emile Tosseau. So, when I was going to get to the, the Wood Crab Boys had a parade or something one day. And here I am up the line, blowing on my bugle, see? Yeah. And the kids all nicknamed me Tosseau. Tosseau used to have the band out of the Spanish Forge. Oh, that's right, I've…

49.t: Emmett Hardy's family and how he started on cornet
49.s: Hazel describes Hardy's musical family and his custom-made convertible trumpet/cornet.
49.ch: Emmett Hardy and the river towns
49.q: Well, his daddy, his daddy was a bass player in the, in the shrine band. Here, you see, and that's where, and his mother played piano. And, uh, they used to sit around at home and play, and that's how he, he never did play, well, he played, he started with a guitar. And a banjo.

879.t: Trombone lessons, school bands, first jobs and post office rally
879.s: Lessons from age 11 on valve then slide trombone, school bands and St. Augustine, joining the union at 17, the Toppers, Dejan's band, and the Zip Codes playing political rallies.
879.q: Oh, yeah, I started taking music lessons, uh, when I was about 11 years old. Uh, started out on the vowel trombone. I played the vowel trombone for, uh, uh, four years. And, uh, the reason why my daddy put me on the vowel trombone, because he figured my arm wasn't long enough for the slide to go…

290.t: First violin and drums, then trumpet with Maurice Duran and Professor Nicholson
290.s: No one else in his family played; he tried violin in 1913, then trap drums, then learned trumpet fingering from Maurice Duran and studied with Professor Nicholson.
290.q: took the music. And I started, I guess you'd like to know that, started trying to play a violin. And that was around in 1913. So I tried to play a violin when I kept it a couple of months with an instructor, somebody tried to show me. And I couldn't do anything with that. So then I changed my mind,…

54.t: Born in Natchez; first music heard and first horns in town
54.s: McAllister was born in Natchez, heard guitar young, and is 78. The first horn player in town was trombonist Frank Brakely; Bud's son later mastered sax.
54.q: No, sir. The first one came in here was the colored fellow by the name of Frank Brakely. He played trombone. Trombone was first. Then the little short cornet. And then people began to add sax. And Bud's son, I know he ran away from the band at one time, and he decided he would, he thought within…

300.t: Grandfather's music lessons, learning bass and trombone
300.s: Humphrey's grandfather taught music in the house; he started on bass, then trombone, and followed Kid Ory and Kid Oliver.
300.q: Yeah. That's where we lived at. Mm-hmm. My aunt practically took care of us. Mm-hmm. And my grandfather was a musician, you know, a music teacher.

58.t: Practice habits and how Punch got into the plantation band
58.s: Punch tells of an hour's practice a day and moving from drum to valve trombone, baritone and cornet in the band.
58.q: Oh, well, when I first picked up horn, I wouldn't have, but no time to practice at 12 o'clock in the day when I come from work. Uh-huh. Practice at 12 o'clock in the day and again at night when I get off, see? Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And on Sundays when we get on the corners, they call it, everybody had a…

127.t: No regrets, and learning bass drum and horn in the country
127.s: Punch says he never wanted to do anything but play music, and ran away from cutting cane. Working in the fields, Punch got the bass drum from the town brass band and taught himself horn; he says he taught Red Allen and Red's father taught him.
127.q: No but I'll tell you Dick got all this down See Because old men's had a brass band Well when they bought new instruments They gave all us the old instruments And what you reckon they gave me? The bass drum But I was so happy You know I'd pick up a horn Play something on it every day Borrow his horn…

476.t: First tunes learned; taking up the trumpet for his daughter's school band
476.s: He cannot recall his first ukulele or banjo tunes, but remembers learning trumpet on Sister Kate after buying a horn for his daughter, about 1938.
476.q: My first piece on the trumpet, I remember that clearly. My first piece on the trumpet was, Wish I Could See Me Like My Sister Kate.

574.t: Taking up trombone after the First World War
574.s: The band ran out of trombone players so he took it up; the band owned the instruments; he moved to New Orleans in 1921.
574.q: Did you have a teacher on trombone? When I came here I had a teacher. Mm-hmm. About seventh That's around about 1918. Were you still living up there in Thibodeau then? No, we're living in Thibodeau. I didn't come down here until 1921. Did you have a teacher on trombone? When I came here I had a…

639.t: Buying his first cornet from the Sears catalog
639.s: He saved six months to buy a 6.95 cornet from Sears and taught himself from the instruction book. He talks about cornet versus trumpet and his mouthpieces.
639.q: to go back around 1909 or 1910. Must have started around 1909. and I saw this little boy playing clarinet, and it, oh, boy, it affected me terribly. He was in the street parade, and I just wanted to get in the street parade band so badly. So I began worrying my folks about getting me a cornet, and…

767.t: Boys band in Brenham and summers with Sid Isles in Houston
767.s: Harris, born in Brenham, Texas, starts music at 13-14 in a boys band under Gus Allen (Uncle Beansy), moves from alto horn to slide trombone, and spends summers playing and learning band management with Sid Isles.
767.ch: Early years in Brenham and Houston
767.q: I'm L.D. Harris. My real name is Lawrence Douglas Harris. I was born and raised in Brenham, Texas. That's about 165 miles from here. It's on H and T.C. between Austin and Houston, Texas. And I started out playing music between the ages of 13 and 14, started studying music. They organized a boys…

201.t: Choosing the trombone as a boy
201.s: His father steered him to trombone over trumpet, his mother bought a pawn-shop horn, and teacher Bill Cully encouraged him.
201.ch: Childhood, Berklee and the Air Force
201.q: Yes I did as a matter of fact. I can start at the beginning if you want. I don’t want to get too lengthy with this. I can get lengthy but, I came home from public school I think in the fourth or fifth grade and they had passed out this piece of paper about taking an instrument and a group thing and…

673.s: Cooper started on drums, idolized his cousin in Erskine Hawkins's band, wanted baseball, then got a trombone from his dad.
673.q: Well that’s one of the great parts about music, is you never know it all. Always, every day something is learned.

154.t: Growing up in the Bronx and Mount Vernon; getting a Wurlitzer trombone
154.s: No musical family; school band, alto horn, bass drum, then a broken-umbrella trombone and a cheap Wurlitzer horn.
154.q: Not really. You see I grew up in the Bronx. Then when I was ten I moved to Mount Vernon. And in the Bronx they didn’t have any band so I didn’t know where that radio, the radio stuff came from. I heard the radio and I heard music but I didn’t know anything about it. So then when I got to Mount…

203.t: Taking up the cornet and trumpet in 1926
203.s: Best explains how a school cornet led to a Buescher trumpet, and why he quit piano lessons.
203.q: And it goes back to 1926. My brother brought a cornet home from the public schools and I picked it up one day and it had a little book with the fingering on it and I could play “My Country Tis of Thee.” Well it wound up that I took the cornet. The music professor needed a trombone player, and he…

981.t: First instruments: piano, accordion, doo-wop, then tuba in school
981.s: Fleming moves from piano and accordion to doo-wop, then teaches himself tuba at 13 and gets school upright bass lessons. His uncle had promised him gigs if he had a bass.
981.q: Okay. My first instrument was piano and I just realized that in my community, as six year olds we had a band. All right. Later I went to accordion. When I went to accordion I had fantasies and visions of playing in front of people. And I just had visions of myself doing that. After that, after I…

210.t: Learning publicity: English major and instinct
210.s: Jacobs studied English and learned publicity instinctively, trusted by the artists she worked with.
210.q: My uncle was a very, very clever man and very, very good. And he gave me a lot of freedom. You know he just let me do it. And I guess I just did it. But of course I did have an education, I majored in English, I primarily wanted to be a journalist or a librarian, and as far as publicity went I just…

842.t: Choosing Hamilton, Eddie Condon, and buying McNally's trombone
842.s: His father took him to Condon's; he calls Emerson Brown about the Hamilton Dixieland band and buys McNally's 1932 Martin trombone.
842.q: A good one. Although he didn’t last that long in high school music. In any event, so that’s about the time that I decided I wanted to go to Hamilton College. And I heard — great they had a Dixieland band. And I’d been listening. I was kind of brought up as a swing player but I’d been listening to…

347.t: Finding a leaky trumpet at Henry P. Archer School
347.s: At about eleven he gets a leaky trumpet from the school attic; he wanted a sax but could not afford the mouthpiece.
347.q: I was eleven years old, and what grade was I, maybe the fifth grade. Because I started school at seven, not six. Back then six was the starting grade for poor people. There was no kindergarten for most people. They couldn’t afford it. So they started at six. But I was sickly, very sick when I was…

596.t: Lecture-demonstrations and starting trombone at twelve
596.s: He has given lecture-demonstrations for decades, and recalls taking up trombone at 12 with teacher Eddie Pearson and a boyhood band with Vernell Fournier.
596.q: For 35 years. I’ve done — or maybe 40 — I’ve done what’s called a lecture- demonstration. I think Billy Taylor started this in the 60s, where we lecture and we demonstrate. And I’ve been doing that constantly, every year, because for me it’s been like a commitment. Naturally education — I’ve done…

813.t: Starting on banjo, piano, clarinet and trombone before drums
813.s: He tried several instruments, ended on drums because of braces, and says he would go back to trombone.
813.q: No. That’s what I wound up with. I started with banjo, then piano, clarinet, trombone, and I’d probably still be playing that if I didn’t have to have braces. And drums was something convenient to play that your teeth can be bound up and it doesn’t really matter. And I just stayed with drums. With…

366.t: Radio, his father and his first clarinets
366.s: Sol's father wanted a grocery store but bought him an $8 Albert system clarinet then a Penzer Mueller.
366.q: Yes my father bought me my first clarinet, believe it or not it was an Albert System clarinet. I still think I have the receipt. We bought it in a pawn shop for $8. An Albert system. Then we bought a Penzer Mueller clarinet. There’s an article I gave you, Monk, in 1935 a Penzer Mueller clarinet for…

85.t: Meeting cousin Cuban Bennett in McDonald, Pennsylvania
85.s: Carter was sent to McDonald, PA at eleven, where he heard Cuban Bennett's lyrical trumpet, which he wanted to sound like.
85.q: Well, I met Cuban first about nineteen twenty . . . oh, I met him when I was eleven years old, because my folks sent me away from New York to McDonald, Pennsylvania, which is where my mother’s brother, my Uncle Saunders, lived. He was the father of Cuban, as I said, and they wanted to get me away…

470.t: First instruments: trombone, E-flat tuba and the cigar-box fingering
470.s: In seventh grade he was handed a tuba instead of a trombone, lugged it home on the streetcar, and later got a sousaphone from Mr. Brown at Attucks.
470.ch: Crispus Attucks and the Indiana Avenue scene
470.q: Seventh grade. They brought us instruments and asked us what instrument we wanted to play. Sometimes they looked at us and looked at our physical equipment. If you had big lips, they wanted you to play this; little lips, they wanted you to play that, which was really strange. I guess that took some…

144.t: Learning on the baritone horn alongside the trombone
144.s: Fuller borrowed a school baritone horn, learned positions on it, and transferred this to the slide trombone; he compares fixed and open instruments.
144.q: Well, I tried it out. The kid that had the baritone horn in school didn’t like it and wouldn’t practice it. When we went there to get the issue of our respected instruments, that baritone would always be there. A couple of days, I borrowed it and I liked it. I learned that the sound of it was…

108.t: Getting serious: bugle calls, school orchestras and trumpet
108.s: School bugle calls and orchestras make him serious; his cornet wears out and he moves to a used Holton trumpet; his mother's encouragement.
108.ch: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
108.q: Oh, no. When I was in elementary school, on certain holidays, like the military holidays, the Fourth of July, or Armistice Day, or something like that, they would have

464.t: Al Henshaw's broken trumpet and the Christmas 1953 gift
464.s: A neighbor going to Korea gives him a defective trumpet; his music teacher spots it and his father buys a new one.
464.q: Well, yes, because from my very beginning, the kids in the neighborhood, we had a friend. His name was Al Henshaw, and Al was in the service. He was a career person in the service; he was getting ready to go to Korea. Before he decided to leave, he gathered all the kids from the neighborhood that…

506.t: The aluminum cello and finding your sound
506.s: Carter discusses his first aluminum cello, its aggressive sound and his approach to finding and keeping an instrument's sound.
506.q: Yeah, but it had a great sound. As a matter of fact, they still make those things. According to one of the events in the past two years, Yo-Yo Ma was playing outside, like in a White House event, with an aluminum cello equivalent to that. He's endorsing it the best. Fifty years late for me, because…

80.t: Leaving Calhoun for Pittsburgh and the Arban book
80.s: He joined his brother Theophilus in Pittsburgh, where an insurance man gave him a large Arban trumpet method book in 1924.
80.q: Uh-huh, and as soon as we could I got a hold of a trumpet, and one of those big Arbon books, Italian insurance man, he came in one day and saw me playing and he said, 'You play the trumpet?' I said, well, he said, 'Play something.' So I played. He said, 'I'm going to bring you something.' Next time…

145.s: Their uncle began Ernie on trumpet at about seven, then he studied with George Pacheco.
145.ch: Family follow-ups from the first reels
145.q: My uncle Ernest gave him a trumpet and started him out, teaching him on the trumpet. So, my uncle Ernest was my brother Ernie's first teacher on the trumpet. After that, after he taught him all that he could teach him, he made arrangements to have a teacher that was formerly one of the solo trumpet…

4.t: Learning instruments from Johnny; Johnny's composing and arranging
4.s: Johnny started Reb on trumpet and saxophone along with drums and wrote his first march at thirteen; Spikes shows a picture of Johnny directing a concert band.
4.ch: San Francisco, the So Different Orchestra and Johnny
4.q: Oh, when I started playing drums, that was the beginning. My brother started me right on the rest of them soon as I got the drums, you know. He started me on trumpet and saxophone and I was playing all these other things before he even played the saxophone and trumpet. He had some of these…

166.t: Earl Bostic and how he came to play trumpet
166.s: Earl Bostic got a clarinet from the church; Simmons wanted a saxophone but only trumpets were left.
166.ch: Childhood in Oklahoma, Kansas City and Tulsa
166.q: So, how I started playing trumpet. Earl Bostic was a very gifted young man. He would appear on Saturday night, amateur shows, you know, and he'd play the part of Harold Teen. He had the big leg pants and he'd whistle and play ukelele. win first prize And he'd always (unintelligible). So, he was a…

379.t: Machin's quartet and picking up the trumpet
379.s: With Machin needing a trumpeter, he buys a pawnshop horn for fifteen dollars, learns it in weeks and records La Parumbeda.
379.q: I worked with him (inaudible) and I played with him (inaudible), with Noble Sissle and then I left my job, and the guy that was working, that I was substituting, came back to the job. So (inaudible) Sam Wooding came from Paris, and as I was working around with Sam Wooding there was another big band…

70.t: McKinney's Synco Septet and Claude Jones's advice to take up trombone
70.s: He listened to McKinney's septet rehearse; Claude Jones, who married his sister, urged him to take up trombone because good Black trombonists were scarce.
70.ch: Childhood and first bands in Ohio
70.q: Well, McKinney had a band called Synco Cinco Septet. They only had seven pieces. And they used to rehearse out to Milt Senior's house, you know.

18.t: Coming into jazz: sneaking out at night and Jimmy Harrison
18.s: He sneaked out of the dormitory to play for $5-10 a night; he claims no influences but went to hear trombonist Jimmy Harrison.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: Oh, my brother took me in the boarding school so ... I still had a horn and you had to stay on on Saturday night and you had to spend the night when you go in ... so I used to sneak out of the dormitory and go out and play at night and my brother would let me in. And then I got permission and we…

96.t: Deciding to form a band; father teaches them; who played what
96.s: They get instruments, with his father teaching, and assign instruments to the gang; the band forms.
96.ch: Chicago boyhood and the Austin High Gang
96.q: and man we put those on and we listened to those records. King Oliver and Louis Armstrong were blowing and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and we just flipped our heads. And we said, man this is it, jazz, you know.

387.t: Trumpet lessons and his brother's influence
387.s: Harvey Sartorius teaches him trumpet and his brother pushes him toward arranging for the kids' band.
387.q: At that time I guess it must have been late grammar school and I began taking trumpet lessons at Teacher's College by a guy named Harvey Sartorius who became a music teacher on Long Island somewhere. Somebody must remember him, Harvey was quite a guy. He introduced me to a lot of these

74.t: Starting on trombone in the Gibbs High School band
74.s: A grandfather on the instrument committee lets him choose the trombone; he starts in the Little Rock high school band.
74.q: My Grand-dad was the head of a committee that bought up a gang of instruments and gave them to the high schools. By my grand-dad being the head of the committee I had my choice of any instrument I wanted in the band. So, I choose the trombone as a little kid. In fact, I have a little picture of me…

86.t: Taking up the old York cornet and the trombone
86.s: His uncle repaired an old cornet and ordered a mouthpiece; Edison tried trombone but went back to trumpet.
86.q: of his house, you know. Whatever he said, that's what he meant, you know. And it was a fantastic way of growing up. Then I finally started playing the trumpet.

171.t: From trumpet to baritone and tuba in high school
171.s: Air leaked from his lips on trumpet so he moved to baritone horn, then tuba, around age 11-13.
171.ch: Growing up with music in Austin
171.q: So this is what I got from my family and band. When I -- I know I started out on trumpet, but I found I could never -- air was coming out both sides of my lips. I could never get the pressure to bring it through there, so I could only play one octave --
